547.title: Cartloads of books
547.hook: read cartloads of books, but only one thing counts; all else is ego's talk (Asa di Var, ang 467)
547.howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing Gurbani daily, and this salok of Asa di Var, sung at dawn, reminds them that reading is meant to lead to remembering the One, not to a pile of knowledge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what ego is, and your line: ego, and its cure. Did you catch your I jumping to the center, and smile at it? Today, one of the places ego hides best: in what we know. Day five hundred forty-seven.

A list of books to read someday. Podcasts saved for later. Articles opened in tabs and never closed. It's a strange modern condition: drowning in things to know, and still unsure of the main thing. Guru Nanak lived when a book was copied by hand, a precious object. And still he pictured someone with so many books they had to be hauled away in carts. Then he asked what all of it was worth.
screen: `A LIST OF BOOKS TO READ.` → `DROWNING IN THINGS TO KNOW.` → `BOOKS HAULED AWAY IN CARTS.`

segments.voice: The salok is on ang 467, and its pictures pile up on purpose. In paraphrase: you could read and read and fill whole carts with books. You could read and read and load caravans. You could read and fill boats, and fill pits. You could read for years and years, for every month of the year, for your whole life, with every breath. And then the last line drops like a stone. Nanak, only one thing is counted. Ik gal. Everything else is ego's babble. That word, gal, is everyday Punjabi for a thing, a matter, a word said. Only one matter goes into the account. What is it? The salok doesn't spell it out in that line, but Sikh teachers read it as the Name, remembering the One, lived in the heart. And notice what Guru Nanak doesn't say. He doesn't say reading is bad. The Gurus were poets and scholars. Sikh tradition credits Guru Angad with shaping the Gurmukhi script and teaching people to read it. Gurdwaras read from the Guru Granth Sahib every day. The point is about what reading is for. Learning that only makes a bigger pile, a bigger I who knows more, is the ego's talk from yesterday's salok in a new outfit. Learning that leads to one thing, lived, is something else. The very next salok says it sharply: the more one writes and reads, the more one burns. Set beside this salok, the burning is learning that only feeds the self. There's a kind of relief in this. You don't have to get through the whole pile. You only have to let one line actually change you.
screen: `CARTS, CARAVANS, BOATS OF BOOKS.` · `ONLY ONE THING IS COUNTED.` · `READING ISN'T THE PROBLEM.` · `LET ONE LINE CHANGE YOU.` · then, large: `ONE THING COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line deeply. Choose one line you've met on this path. It could be today's: only one thing is counted. Say it to yourself slowly, once. Then say it again, and stop on each word. Notice which word catches. Let the line sit in you without adding commentary, without reaching for the next line. If your mind wants to rush on, come back to the one line. If you pray, you can say Waheguru between the repetitions. The bell holds the time.
Cartloads of books. Guru Nanak's picture of endless reading: carts, caravans and boats of it. Only one thing is counted; the rest is ego's talk.
Your line: one thing counts. Today, before you open one more article or video, ask what one thing you already know but haven't lived yet. Day five hundred forty-seven.

548.title: False king, false subjects
548.hook: false the king, false the subjects, false the whole world, and still we love it (Asa di Var, ang 468)
548.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok of koorh in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh teaching holds that a householder lives fully in the world while knowing that all of it passes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cartloads of books, and your line: one thing counts. What did you already know but hadn't lived yet? Today Guru Nanak looks at everything else we count, and gives it a hard name. Day five hundred forty-eight.

Old cities are full of the leftovers of someone's empire. A gate that once had guards. A palace that is now a museum, with a gift shop where the throne room used to be. Whoever built it surely meant it to stand forever. In Guru Nanak's own lifetime, Punjab watched one ruling house fall and another rise: the Lodi sultans gave way to Babur and the Mughals. Guru Nanak saw power change hands up close. And in the Asa di Var there is a salok that starts with the king himself and works its way down to everything we own and love.
screen: `A PALACE WITH A GIFT SHOP.` → `THRONES CHANGE HANDS.` → `A SALOK THAT STARTS WITH THE KING.`

segments.voice: The word that repeats is koorh, and it runs through the salok on ang 468, phrase after phrase. In paraphrase: koorh is the king, koorh the subjects, koorh the whole world. Koorh are the mansions and palaces, and koorh the ones who live in them. Koorh is gold, koorh is silver, koorh are those who wear them. Koorh is the body, koorh the clothes, koorh the matchless beauty. Koorh is the husband, koorh the wife; they waste away and are gone. Koorh usually gets translated false. But in this salok it means something gentler and sadder than lying. It means what passes. What looks solid and isn't. Gold is real gold, a palace is a real palace, and a marriage is a real marriage, but none of them can hold you up forever. Then comes the turn: and still we love it. The false, the salok says, fall in love with the false and forget the Creator. With whom should we make friends? The whole world is passing away. Falsehood is sweet, falsehood is honey; falsehood drowns boatloads of people. And the salok ends with Nanak's plea to the One: without you, everything is koorh, koorh. Sikh teachers are careful here. Guru Nanak, as Sikhs remember him, was a householder who married, raised a family, and in his later years farmed at Kartarpur. Sikhs aren't asked to leave the world or despise it. The point is where the heart leans its full weight. Love your people, use the silver, live in the house. Just don't mistake any of it for the thing that lasts.
screen: `KOORH: KING, SUBJECTS, WORLD.` · `PALACES, GOLD, BEAUTY, MARRIAGE.` · `KOORH MEANS WHAT PASSES.` · `LIVE IN IT; DON'T LEAN ON IT.` · then, large: `WITHOUT YOU, ALL IS KOORH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one thing that won't last. Look around wherever you are and let your eyes rest on one object you care about: a phone, a mug, a photograph, a ring. Look at it the way you'd look at it if you knew this was the last week you'd have it. Notice any tenderness that comes up, and any grip. Then breathe out, and loosen the grip a little, without letting go of the care. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, the One who doesn't pass. The bell holds the time.
False king. Koorh, the false, the passing: king, subjects, palaces, gold and beauty. Without the One, Guru Nanak says, all of it is koorh.
Your line: it won't last. Today, when something you own breaks or something you wanted slips away, say the line, and notice what's still there. Day five hundred forty-eight.

549.title: When the heart is true
549.hook: truth is known when the heart is true and falsehood's dirt is washed (Asa di Var, ang 468)
549.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok of truth in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikhs often recall Guru Nanak's line in Sri Rag that truth stands above all, and truthful living higher still.

segments.voice: Yesterday, false king, koorh, the passing, and your line: it won't last. What did you notice was still there? Today the very next salok answers koorh with its opposite: sach, truth. Day five hundred forty-nine.

A friend who's being straight with you shows it, and not only in the words. The eyes stay on yours, the shoulders aren't braced, there's no little gap between what's said and what's meant. The opposite shows too, even when every word is technically accurate. Truth, it turns out, isn't only a property of sentences. It's a property of people. Guru Nanak wrote a salok right after yesterday's list of koorh, and it doesn't ask what is true. It asks something harder. When can a person be said to know truth at all?
screen: `A FRIEND BEING STRAIGHT WITH YOU.` → `TRUTH LIVES IN PEOPLE.` → `WHEN DOES A PERSON KNOW IT?`

segments.voice: The salok on ang 468 is built like a ladder, each rung starting the same way: sach taa par jaaneeai. Truth is known only when. Then Guru Nanak fills in the rest. Truth is known when the heart itself is true. When the dirt of falsehood comes off, and the body is washed clean. Truth is known when a person loves truth, when hearing the Name the mind delights, and so finds the door of freedom. Truth is known when a person knows the way to live: making the body into a field and planting the Creator's seed in it. Truth is known when a person takes true teaching, shows kindness to living beings, and gives what they can. Truth is known when a person makes their own self the place of pilgrimage, and settles there, guided by the True Guru. And then the last rung: truth is the medicine for everyone. It washes out wrongdoing. Look at what this list is made of. Not one rung is about winning an argument or holding the right opinion. Every rung is about a person: what the heart loves, how the life is lived, how the hands treat other beings. In Gurbani, sach is both a name for the One and the quality of a life lined up with the One. So a true heart isn't a heart that never makes mistakes. It's a heart with no gap between what it shows and what it is. Yesterday's salok said koorh drowns boatloads. Today's says truth heals everyone. The washing comes first, and it's daily work.
screen: `TRUTH IS KNOWN ONLY WHEN...` · `THE HEART ITSELF IS TRUE.` · `THE BODY A FIELD, THE SEED PLANTED.` · `TRUTH IS MEDICINE FOR ALL.` · then, large: `A TRUE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clean one untruth. Sit and let your breathing settle. Look gently for one small gap between what you show and what is: a white lie you've repeated, a promise you made knowing you wouldn't keep it, a version of yourself you've been performing. Pick just one. Picture washing it, the way you'd wash dirt off your hands. Then decide one small, true thing you could say or do about it today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
When the heart is true. Guru Nanak's ladder of sach: truth is known only when the heart is true, falsehood's dirt is washed, and the life is lived in kindness.
screen: `WHEN THE HEART IS TRUE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a true heart. Today, do the one true thing you chose, and notice how the body feels afterward. Day five hundred forty-nine.

550.title: Pain the medicine
550.hook: pain became the medicine and pleasure the disease (Asa di Var, ang 469)
550.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and many recall dukh daaroo, sukh rog in hard times as a reminder that suffering can turn the heart toward the One.

segments.voice: Yesterday, when the heart is true, and your line: a true heart. Did you do your one true thing? Yesterday's salok ended with truth as medicine. Today's turns the medicine upside down. Day five hundred fifty.

Ask people when they changed the most, and very few will say it was the year everything went well. They'll name the breakup, the layoff, the hospital waiting room, the year a parent died. Nobody would choose those seasons. Nobody should wish them on anyone. And yet, looking back, many people say: that's when I woke up. That's when I found out who my friends were, or what I actually believed. Guru Nanak put that strange experience into one line of the Asa di Var, and it still startles people who hear it.
screen: `WHEN DID YOU CHANGE THE MOST?` → `NOBODY CHOOSES THOSE SEASONS.` → `ONE STARTLING LINE.`

segments.voice: The salok is on ang 469. Its opening line, in paraphrase: pain has become the medicine, and pleasure the disease, because where there is pleasure, there is no longing for you. Dukh daaroo, sukh rog. Dukh is pain, sorrow, suffering. Daaroo is medicine. Sukh is comfort, pleasure, ease. Rog is disease. It's worth slowing down, because this line is easy to misread. Guru Nanak isn't saying pain is good, or that people deserve to suffer, or that anyone should go looking for it. Sikh teaching doesn't praise hurting yourself; the Gurus turned away from harsh self-punishment as a path. And in Sikh life, relieving other people's pain is a duty: the langar feeds the hungry, and Sikhs have long run free kitchens and clinics in disasters. The line is about what comfort can do to the heart. When everything is easy, it's easy to forget the One. Ease can make us sleepy. Pain, the salok says, often does the opposite. It breaks the illusion that we're in control, and it turns the heart toward the One. Then the salok goes on, still in paraphrase: you are the Doer; I am nothing; if I try to do it myself, nothing happens. And then a line that connects back to day five hundred forty-two: I am a sacrifice to you, dwelling in your kudrat, your creation; your limits can't be known. So the medicine isn't the pain itself. It's what pain can open: the end of pretending we run the world, and a turn toward the One who does.
screen: `DUKH DAAROO, SUKH ROG.` · `NOT: PAIN IS GOOD.` · `EASE CAN MAKE US FORGET.` · `YOU ARE THE DOER.` · then, large: `PAIN THE MEDICINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a lesson in one pain. Sit and breathe slowly. Think of a hard season that is now behind you, not the hardest, and not one that still feels raw. If nothing comes, that's fine; just rest in the breath. If one does come, don't relive it. Ask one quiet question: what did that season teach me, or turn me toward? Let the answer be small. A friendship. A habit. A kind of patience. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, for what you learned and for who helped. The bell holds the time.
Pain the medicine. Dukh daaroo, sukh rog: in Guru Nanak's salok, pain can turn the heart toward the One, while ease can make it forget.

Your line: pain the medicine. Today, if something small goes wrong, ask what it's pointing you toward before you push it away. And if someone near you is hurting, be part of their medicine. Day five hundred fifty.

551.title: Sweetness and humility
551.hook: mitthat neevee: sweetness and humility are the essence of all virtue (Asa di Var, ang 470)
551.howItsDone: Sikhs quote mitthat neevee, sweetness and humility, as a summary of Sikh character, and hear it in the dawn singing of Asa di Var.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pain the medicine, and your line: pain the medicine. Did something small that went wrong point you somewhere? Today Guru Nanak names two virtues he calls the essence of all the others. Day five hundred fifty-one.

An old shop scale hangs from a beam, two pans swinging under it. Put something in each pan and let go. One side rises, one side sinks. Which side is heavier? The side that goes down. It sounds too simple to matter. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Nanak as a young storekeeper in Sultanpur, weighing out grain on scales like this one. In the Asa di Var, he turned the old market scale into a line Sikhs still quote today.
screen: `AN OLD SHOP SCALE.` → `WHICH SIDE IS HEAVIER?` → `THE SIDE THAT GOES DOWN.`

segments.voice: The salok is on ang 470. At its center are two words: mitthat and neevee. Mitthat is sweetness, from mittha, sweet, the same word you'd use for sugar or a ripe mango. Neevee is lowliness, humility, being low. Mitthat neevee Nanakaa, the line goes: sweetness and humility, Nanak, are the essence of all virtues and goodness. Not one virtue among many. The essence. Then the salok gives the scale. Everyone bows to themselves, it says, in paraphrase; no one bows to another. But put things on the balance and weigh them: the side that bends low is the heavy one. In the market, heavy means valuable. So the one who bows, who stays low, is the one with real weight. Why sweetness and humility together? Think of what each does without the other. Sweetness without humility can be charm: nice words that are really about being liked. Humility without sweetness can turn sour: a person so busy feeling small that they're cold to everyone. Together, they make someone easy to be near, who doesn't need to be above you and doesn't need to hurt you. The same salok opens with a tree and ends with a warning that bowing can be faked; we'll take both tomorrow. Some Sikhs sum up the whole path with these two words: sweet in speech, low in self. Two words, and a whole day of chances to practice them.
screen: `MITTHAT: SWEETNESS.` · `NEEVEE: HUMILITY.` · `THE SIDE THAT BENDS IS HEAVY.` · `SWEET IN SPEECH, LOW IN SELF.` · then, large: `THE ESSENCE OF ALL VIRTUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak sweetly once. Sit and think of one person you'll talk to today, especially one you tend to be short with. Picture the conversation. Find one sentence you could say more sweetly: softer, kinder, without the edge. Say it in your head a few times until it feels natural. Then picture yourself lower, not smaller, just unhurried and unguarded, like the heavy side of the scale. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Sweetness and humility. Mitthat neevee: in Guru Nanak's salok, the essence of all virtue. On the scale, the side that bends low is the heavy one.
Your line: sweet and humble. Today, say your sweeter sentence to the person you pictured, and let them be right about one small thing. Day five hundred fifty-one.

552.title: The silk-cotton tree
552.hook: the silk-cotton tree is tall and straight, but its fruit is tasteless and its leaves useless (Asa di Var, ang 470)
552.howItsDone: Sikhs hear the salok of the simmal tree in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and teachers use it to describe a life that looks impressive but gives nothing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sweetness and humility, and your line: sweet and humble. How did your sweeter sentence land? Today we go back to the start of that same salok, where Guru Nanak points at a tree. Day five hundred fifty-two.

In parts of North India and Punjab, there's a tree that's hard to miss when it blooms. Its branches are bare, and then suddenly they're covered in huge red flowers, so bright they look painted on. It stands tall and straight, often taller than everything around it. In Punjabi it's the simmal. In English it's called the silk-cotton tree, for the fluffy cotton in its pods. People in Guru Nanak's world knew it well. And he used it to open the salok we met yesterday, as a picture of a certain kind of life.
screen: `RED FLOWERS ON BARE BRANCHES.` → `TALL AND STRAIGHT.` → `THE SIMMAL TREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the salok's opening on ang 470, in paraphrase. The simmal tree is straight as an arrow, very tall and very thick. But the birds that come to it full of hope go away disappointed. Its fruits are tasteless, its flowers sickly, and its leaves are of no use. That's the whole picture, and it's sharp. From a distance, the tree has everything: height, straightness, a trunk you can't get your arms around, a blaze of color. A bird flying over would think, there's my meal, there's my shade. It lands, and finds nothing to eat, no shade worth sitting in, nothing that feeds. The tree isn't wicked. It just isn't useful. And then, right after the tree, come the lines we heard yesterday: sweetness and humility are the essence of virtue; the side of the scale that bends low is the heavy one. So the tree is the opposite of the scale. It's all height and no weight. All show and no fruit. The salok keeps going, too. It describes the guilty one who bows twice as low, the way a hunter crouches to stalk a deer. Low, but not humble. And then it asks: what's the use of bowing the head if the heart stays impure? Put together, the lesson is about what people come to us for. Someone in trouble doesn't need us to be impressive. They need fruit: a meal, a kind word, real shade. The salok measures a life by what it gives, not how tall it stands.
screen: `TALL, STRAIGHT, THICK, BRIGHT.` · `THE BIRDS LEAVE DISAPPOINTED.` · `ALL HEIGHT, NO WEIGHT.` · `PEOPLE NEED FRUIT, NOT HEIGHT.` · then, large: `USEFUL, NOT TALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be useful, not just tall. Sit and breathe. Picture the people who might come to you this week, hoping for something: a coworker, a child, a friend, a neighbor. For each one, ask what fruit they'd actually need. Not a performance, not advice to look clever, but something that feeds: time, help, a listening ear. Choose one small fruit you can give today. Hold that picture for a few breaths. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
The silk-cotton tree. Guru Nanak's simmal: tall, straight and bright, but the birds that come to it in hope leave with nothing.
Your line: useful, not tall. Today, give your one fruit to the person you pictured, and don't mention it on any feed. Day five hundred fifty-two.

553.title: Sacrifice to the Guru
553.hook: satgur vittahu vaariaa: a sacrifice to the Guru, meeting whom I remember the Master (Asa di Var, ang 470)
553.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this pauri in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and express gratitude to the Guru daily in Ardas and in bowing before the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the silk-cotton tree, and your line: useful, not tall. Who got your fruit? It's a week's end, too: ego and its cure, cartloads of books, the false king, the true heart, pain the medicine, sweetness, the tree. Today, the pauri that gathers them. Day five hundred fifty-three.
screen: `USEFUL, NOT TALL.` · `A WEEK: EGO, BOOKS, KOORH, TRUTH, SWEETNESS.`

segments.voice: A single sentence that rearranged everything. A book picked up by accident. A stranger on a train. Some lives turn on one afternoon like that. Ask what changed, though, and the answer is rarely the world. The street was the same street, the job the same job. What changed was the seeing. Back on day five hundred thirty-eight, Guru Nanak said he'd give himself a hundred times a day to the Guru who made angels out of men. Today's pauri comes back to that gratitude, and says exactly what changed.
screen: `A SENTENCE, A BOOK, A STRANGER.` → `THE SAME STREET, THE SAME JOB.` → `WHAT CHANGED WAS THE SEEING.`

segments.voice: The pauri is on ang 470, the same page as the tree and the scale. It opens: satgur vittahu vaariaa. I am a sacrifice to the True Guru. Vaariaa is a word of love and offering, the feeling behind the custom of circling something precious around a loved one's head and giving it away. Then, in paraphrase: meeting the Guru, I remembered the Master. The Guru gave the ointment of wisdom, and with these same eyes I now see the world as it is. Gian anjan. Anjan is the dark ointment people put along the eyes. The eyes don't change. What they can see does. That's the turning point. Before, the world was koorh, the false king and the tall tree, all looking solid and impressive. After, the same world is seen clearly, with the One in it. Then the pauri warns about the other road. Traders who leave the Master and attach to another, it says, are drowned. And it ends with a picture: the True Guru is the boat, though few realize it, and by grace the Guru carries people across. In Sikh teaching, the Guru is the One's word reaching a person: through the human Gurus, and now through the Guru Granth Sahib. In this pauri, the sacrifice is gratitude: offering yourself to whatever opened your eyes, and keeping them open. This week's saloks were all about seeing: ego, books, koorh, truth, pain, sweetness, the tree. Here's what lets you see them.
screen: `VAARIAA: I OFFER MYSELF.` · `GIAN ANJAN: WISDOM ON THE EYES.` · `THE SAME EYES, A NEW WORLD.` · `THE GURU IS THE BOAT.` · then, large: `THE TURNING POINT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a turning point. Sit and breathe out slowly. Let one moment come back when your way of seeing changed: a person, a line, a day. Picture the before and the after. Notice what you see now that you couldn't see then. If gratitude comes, let it come, toward the person, the moment, or, if you pray, toward the One behind them. If you'd like, you can say Waheguru, softly, as a thank-you. The bell holds the time.
Sacrifice to the Guru. Satgur vittahu vaariaa: I offer myself to the True Guru, who put wisdom on my eyes, so I see the same world truly.
Your line: the turning point. Today, look at one familiar thing, your street, your kitchen, a face, as if the ointment were fresh on your eyes, and see what's there. Day five hundred fifty-three.

fork.setup: you've met the Guru and your eyes have been opened. what does the pauri say you now see?
options: a different world, far from this one.
this same world, seen as it really is.
nothing; the eyes close in meditation.
fork.reveal: the Guru gave the ointment of wisdom, and with these eyes the world is seen. the eyes don't change; what they see does.

original.note: Gurmukhi: I am a sacrifice to the True Guru; the opening of the pauri.

trapdoor: what you thought: sacrifice means giving something up.
what it means: offering yourself in gratitude to the Guru who opened your eyes to the same world, seen truly.
what a scholar hears: vaarna is the gesture of circling something around a loved one and giving it away; the pauri pairs it with gian anjan, wisdom's eye-salve.
